$comment: Pins the Go and TypeScript matchers to one another on how the occurrences of a repeated requirement id pair up. Both halves read this file and assert the same expectations, including the ORDER of the result, so the two engines cannot disagree about what a comparison contains. A requirement id names the requirement rather than the finding (maintainer ruling, 2026-09-20), so a repeated id is legal and expected; occurrences pair by the composite content key of code, title and affectedPackages, with document position as the tie-break (maintainer ruling, 2026-11-23). Matched pairs are named by title because a title is unique within each side of every case below, except where the case is deliberately about indistinguishable occurrences.

cases.name: identical occurrences on both sides
cases.why: A document compared with an identical copy of itself must report no change; before 2026-11-23 every occurrence was reported absent AND new.

cases.name: the new side is reordered
cases.why: Nothing in hdf-schema orders requirements[], so content decides and a producer that reorders its output reports no change. Emitted in the OLD side's order.

cases.name: a surplus occurrence on the new side
cases.why: One more finding against the same requirement is new, and does not disturb the occurrence that was already there.

cases.name: a surplus occurrence on the old side
cases.why: One finding resolved while the other persists: absent, not a wholesale replacement.

cases.name: three occurrences against one
cases.why: N to M with N greater than M: the content match is kept and the rest are absent, in document order.

cases.name: one occurrence against three
cases.why: N to M with N less than M, and the content match is not the first in document order — a positional rule would pair B with A here.

cases.name: equal counts, one occurrence changed
cases.why: N equals M but the content does not all match: the content pair is kept and the remainder pairs positionally, so a changed occurrence is reported as a change rather than as absent plus new.

cases.name: occurrences separated only by affectedPackages
cases.whyPairingNotAsserted: Titles are equal here on purpose; the point is that no occurrence is lost when only affectedPackages differs, which is the shipped dropwizard case.
cases.why: One CVE reported against two packages: affectedPackages is the only discriminator in the shipped cyclonedx golden.

cases.name: indistinguishable occurrences
cases.whyPairingNotAsserted: The occurrences are interchangeable, so which pairs with which cannot be observed and is not asserted.
cases.why: Two entries that no content key can separate — the shipped inspec overlay repeats, which differ only in a timestamp's microseconds. Their keys are EQUAL, so they pair through that key's queue in document order; the cross-key positional fallback is reached only by 'equal counts, one occurrence changed'.

cases.name: distinct ids are unaffected
cases.why: The ordinary case still emits in the old side's order, so the change to duplicate handling does not move anything else.

cases.name: mapped id with occurrences on both sides
cases.why: A renumbering carries its occurrences across: the mapping settles the id, the content key settles which occurrence is which.

cases.name: two mapped sources pointing at one target
cases.why: Two ids merged into one: only one old entry can claim the single new occurrence, and the other is absent rather than matched twice.
